subject: Computer Networking
title: What Is the Internet?
description: Learn What Is the Internet? in one minute.

hook.text: Billions of devices talk to each other every second. That global conversation is the internet.

buildup.text: It's not one network. It's thousands of networks — home, office, mobile — all linked together.

discovery.text: No single company owns it. Internet service providers agree to exchange traffic at shared hubs.

twist.text: The internet isn't the web. The web rides on top of the internet, like mail rides on roads.

climax.text: Streaming, gaming, email, apps — they're all separate services traveling on the same global network.

punchline.text: The internet is a network of networks. That's it.

quiz.question: What is the internet, at its core?
options: A website owned by a tech company

details.summary: The internet is a global network of interconnected networks that communicate using standardized protocols. It is not a single entity but a vast mesh of private, public, academic, and government networks linked by copper, fiber, and wireless connections spanning the globe.
details.whyItMatters: The internet underpins modern civilization. Understanding what it actually is demystifies every online experience and reveals why connectivity failures happen.
takeaways: The internet is a network of networks, not a single system
Standardized protocols enable diverse networks to communicate
No single entity owns or controls the entire internet

faq.question: Who owns the internet?
faq.answer: No one owns the entire internet. Different organizations own pieces: ISPs own access networks, companies own data centers, governments control some infrastructure. Standards bodies like IETF coordinate protocols. The internet works because everyone agrees to follow shared rules.

faq.question: Is the internet the same as the World Wide Web?
faq.answer: No. The internet is the physical and logical infrastructure connecting devices worldwide. The web is one application that runs on top of the internet using HTTP and browsers. Email, streaming, gaming, and messaging also run on the internet but are not the web.
